topics.title: US Supreme Court Blocks Trump's IEEPA Tariffs

subtopics.title: IEEPA: Origin and Emergency Powers
subtopics.summary: The International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) was enacted in 1977 by President Jimmy Carter to replace the Trading with Enemy Act of 1917. It is primarily a sanctions tool and not a general tariff law. The President can use it only after formally declaring a National Emergency over an unusual and extraordinary threat originating outside the United States.
facts: Enacted in 1977 by President Jimmy Carter
Replaced the Trading with Enemy Act (1917)
Primarily a sanctions tool, not a general tariff law
President must formally declare a National Emergency first
Threat must originate outside the United States
Can freeze foreign assets held in the US
Can block trade with specific countries, entities or individuals
77 national emergencies declared under IEEPA; 46 ongoing as of Sept 2025

subtopics.title: Supreme Court Verdict on IEEPA Tariffs
subtopics.summary: The Supreme Court struck down President Trump's IEEPA tariffs by a 6-3 verdict. Chief Justice John Roberts held that IEEPA does not allow unilateral tariff actions without Congressional approval. The ruling invalidated the Liberation Day tariffs and raised questions about refunds of tariffs already collected.
facts: Verdict: 6-3 against Trump's IEEPA tariffs
Chief Justice John Roberts clarified the Court's reasoning
'Regulate' under IEEPA does not mean 'Tax'
IEEPA cannot serve as broad authority for imposing tariffs
Any such measures require Congressional authorisation
Liberation Day tariffs (executive order of 02 April 2025) invalidated
Ruling raises questions on refunds of previously collected tariffs
Majority: Roberts, Gorsuch, Barrett, Sotomayor, Kagan, Jackson
Dissent: Thomas, Alito, Kavanaugh

subtopics.title: Alternative Tariff Laws After the Ruling
subtopics.summary: The booklet lists several statutes as legal alternatives to IEEPA for imposing tariffs. Section 122 of the Trade Act 1974 allows temporary tariffs, and the President used it to impose a 10% temporary tariff on goods from all countries. Other options are Section 338 of the Tariff Act 1930, Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act 1962 and Section 301 of the Trade Act 1974.
facts: Section 122, Trade Act 1974: temporary tariffs up to 15% for up to 150 days
Section 122 aims to protect domestic industries and address trade imbalances
10% temporary tariff imposed on goods from all countries under Section 122
Section 338, Tariff Act 1930: import tariffs up to 50%
Section 338 targets countries with discriminatory trade practices
Section 232, Trade Expansion Act 1962: import restrictions on goods threatening national security
Section 232 has been applied to steel and aluminium
Section 301, Trade Act 1974: action against foreign regulations that unfairly burden US trade

subtopics.title: India's Impact and the 2026 Trade Deal
subtopics.summary: The rollback of Liberation Day tariffs benefits nearly 55% of India's exports to the US, which had faced an 18% levy. These goods now face only standard Most-Favoured Nation (MFN) tariff rates, while Section 232 duties remain in force. The 2026 India-US trade deal includes Indian commitments on energy, technology and agricultural trade.
facts: Nearly 55% of India's exports to the US benefit from the rollback
Those goods previously faced an 18% levy
Benefiting goods are now subject only to standard MFN tariff rates
Section 232 tariffs of 50% on steel and aluminium remain in force
25% Section 232 tariff on select automotive components remains in force
25% penalty for purchasing Russian oil has been eliminated
India commits to massive procurement of US energy, technology and agricultural products
India aims to remove barriers for US agricultural exports such as cotton and nuts

subtopics.title: US Congress and India-US Relations
subtopics.summary: The US Congress is a bicameral legislature, and the Supreme Court ruling makes Congressional approval necessary for broad tariffs. India-US total trade reached USD 129.2 billion in 2024, with India's exports to the US larger than its imports from the US. The US is India's third largest investor.
facts: US Congress is bicameral: House of Representatives and Senate
House has 435 seats; members are elected for 2 years
Senate has 100 seats; every state has 2 seats
Senators are elected for 6 years; one-third of Senate seats are up every 2 years
Republican Party has secured 54 Senate seats
India-US total trade in 2024: USD 129.2 billion
India's exports to US in 2024: USD 87.4 billion
India's imports from US in 2024: USD 41.8 billion
USA is India's 3rd largest investor, with FDI inflows of USD 65.19 billion (2000-2024)

subtopics.title: New START Expiry and Its Implications
subtopics.summary: The New START Treaty, the last legally binding nuclear arms control pact between the United States and Russia, expired on 5 February 2026. Its lapse removes binding limits on strategic nuclear arsenals and weakens the verification mechanisms that once made them predictable. Negotiations have stalled as relations deteriorate, and the booklet warns of greater uncertainty, miscalculation and a possible arms race.
facts: Full name: New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START).
Signed in 2010 and came into force in 2011; extended by 5 years in 2021, valid until 05 Feb 2026.
Caps each country at 1550 operationally deployed strategic nuclear warheads.
The ceiling covers deployed warheads only, not stockpiled or reserve weapons.
Russia suspended New START participation in 2023 amid the Ukraine war.
Russia suspended information-sharing on its nuclear forces; the US accuses Russia of non-compliance.
Expiry removes binding caps and halts inspections and nuclear data sharing.
Loss of verification increases opacity and risks eroding global nuclear restraint norms.

subtopics.title: Cold War Arms Control Milestones
subtopics.summary: Arms control between the United States and the Soviet Union progressed through a series of talks and agreements. The SALT I round produced the Anti-Ballistic Missile (ABM) Treaty, which limited missile defence to preserve mutual vulnerability. Later instruments such as SALT II, START I, START II and SORT set quantitative limits or served as interim pacts, but several were never ratified or were later abandoned.
facts: SALT I (1969-1972) resulted in the Anti-Ballistic Missile (ABM) Treaty.
The ABM Treaty restricted deployment of missile defence systems to preserve mutual vulnerability.
SALT II (1972-1979) set quantitative limits on nuclear delivery systems, including long-range missiles and strategic bombers.
The United States never ratified SALT II, owing to Soviet military intervention in Afghanistan.
START I (1991) capped 6000 nuclear warheads, enforced inspections and expired in 2009.
START II (1993) aimed to reduce nuclear weapons to 3,500; Russia withdrew after the US exited the ABM Treaty.
SORT (2002), also known as the Moscow Treaty, was an interim agreement between the US and Russia.

subtopics.title: Nuclear Treaties and Control Regimes
subtopics.summary: Beyond the US-Russia pacts, a set of global treaties and voluntary export-control regimes aims to limit nuclear weapons and their spread. The NPT classifies states as nuclear-weapon or non-nuclear-weapon states, the CTBT seeks to end nuclear testing, and the TPNW bans nuclear weapons outright. Export regimes such as the Australia Group, the MTCR and the Wassenaar Arrangement coordinate controls on sensitive goods.
facts: Outer Space Treaty (1967) bans deployment of weapons of mass destruction in outer space; all nuclear-armed nations are signatories.
NPT (1968) aims to prevent nuclear spread and promote disarmament, and classifies nations as nuclear-weapon or non-nuclear-weapon states.
CTBT (1996) seeks to ban all nuclear weapon testing for civilian and military use.
CTBT is signed by 185 countries and ratified by 170, but remains non-operational as ratification by key nuclear-armed states is pending.
TPNW (2017) bans development, testing, possession and use of nuclear weapons.
Missile Technology Control Regime (1987) is an informal political understanding with 35 members.
Australia Group (1985) is an informal export control forum formed after chemical weapons use in the Iran-Iraq War.
Wassenaar Arrangement (1996) is a voluntary export control regime with 42 members.

subtopics.title: India's Nuclear Journey and the IAEA
subtopics.summary: India's nuclear programme began with the Atomic Energy Commission under Homi J. Bhabha and grew through its reactors and Pokhran tests. Its diplomacy includes a No First Use pledge and a 2008 NSG waiver that enabled nuclear trade despite its non-signatory status to the NPT. The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), established in 1957, supports safeguards, nuclear safety and peaceful use worldwide.
facts: Establishment of the Atomic Energy Commission in 1948 laid the foundation of India's nuclear programme under Homi J. Bhabha.
The Apsara reactor became operational in 1956 as Asia's first nuclear reactor.
Tarapur Atomic Power Station began operations in 1969 as India's first commercial nuclear power plant.
Pokhran-I, 'Smiling Buddha', was conducted on 18 May 1974 at the Pokhran range.
Pokhran-II in May 1998 comprised three tests on 11 May (codename Shakti-I) and two more on 13 May.
India's No First Use policy pledges no first nuclear strike but retains the right to retaliate if attacked.
A 2008 NSG waiver enabled nuclear trade with India despite its non-signatory status to the NPT.
IAEA, established 1957 and headquartered in Vienna, has 180 members and is led by Director General Rafael Grossi.

topics.title: Tarique Rahman Becomes Bangladesh's Next PM

subtopics.title: Tarique Rahman's Rise and Oath
subtopics.summary: Tarique Rahman emerged as the top leader of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) and assumed office as Prime Minister of Bangladesh. He returned to Bangladesh after 17 years and took the oath at Parliament South Plaza in Dhaka. His government succeeded the overthrown government of Sheikh Hasina after 18 months of upheaval.

subtopics.title: 2026 Election Results and Parliament
subtopics.summary: The BNP, led by Tarique Rahman, won the 13th General Election with 209 seats, an absolute majority, ending the Awami League's two-decade dominance. Jamaat-e-Islami emerged as the second-largest party with 68 seats. Bangladesh's legislature is unicameral, with 300 members elected directly and 50 seats reserved for women and allocated proportionally among parties.

subtopics.title: Political Background and Transitions
subtopics.summary: Bangladesh became independent from Pakistan in 1971, and Sheikh Mujibur Rahman became Prime Minister in 1972. Power then passed through Ziaur Rahman, Khaleda Zia and Sheikh Hasina, and the BNP last governed in 2001-2006. The 2024-2026 interim period followed a student-led revolution and Hasina's flight to India.

Sheikh Mujibur Rahman became Prime Minister in 1972

subtopics.title: July National Charter and PM Power Limits
subtopics.summary: The July National Charter (Constitutional Amendment) Implementation Order 2025 is a 28-page reform agreement signed by 25 political parties and the interim government led by Muhammad Yunus. It secured 65.3% yes votes in a referendum. It caps a PM's lifetime service at 10 years, bars the PM from holding both party and government head roles, and creates a two-house parliament.
facts: 28-page constitutional reform agreement
Signed by 25 political parties and the interim government led by Muhammad Yunus
Referendum: 65.3% yes votes against a 50%+1 threshold
First referendum since 1991
No individual can serve as PM for more than 10 years in a lifetime
PM cannot be both party head and head of government
Emergency declaration needs written consent of the cabinet and the leader of the opposition
Bicameral parliament: 400-seat Lower House and new 100-seat Upper House
Reserved seats for women in the Lower House increased to 100
Article 70 to be removed or significantly weakened

subtopics.title: India-Bangladesh Ties Under the New Government
subtopics.summary: Ties between India and Bangladesh moved from strained relations in 2001-2006 to a 'Golden Chapter' under Sheikh Hasina from 2009 to 2024. After Hasina's flight to India, anti-India sentiment surged in Bangladesh. The booklet lists security priorities, including the Hasina extradition issue and avoiding drift toward Pakistan or China, alongside trade and connectivity goals.
facts: 2001-2006: India accused the regime of sheltering ULFA and NDFB
2009-2024 'Golden Chapter' under Sheikh Hasina
Land Boundary Agreement signed in 2015
Interim period saw anti-India sentiment surge

Security priority: counter anti-India extremism and insurgency
Bangladesh is India's biggest trade partner in South Asia
Trade in FY 2023-24 was US$14.01 billion

topics.title: Manipur Gets Elected Government After President's Rule

subtopics.title: New Government in Manipur
subtopics.summary: President Droupadi Murmu revoked President's Rule in Manipur after nearly one year, clearing the path for an elected government. Yumnam Khemchand Singh (BJP) was sworn in as the 13th Manipur Chief Minister. Two Deputy Chief Ministers, Nemcha Kipgen and Losii Dikho, took oath alongside him.

President's Rule in Manipur had lasted nearly one year
Yumnam Khemchand Singh (BJP) sworn in as 13th Manipur CM

subtopics.title: Kuki-Zomi and Meitei Violence
subtopics.summary: Violence erupted between Kuki-Zomi tribals and the Meitei community, the first clash of its kind in three decades in Manipur. A key trigger was the Meitei demand for Scheduled Tribe (ST) status, which has persisted since 2012. A 2023 High Court direction to consider that request added to tensions with Kuki groups.

State withdrew from suspension of operations agreement with KNA and ZRA in March 2023

subtopics.title: Historical Background and Divides
subtopics.summary: Meiteis make up 52 per cent of Manipur's population and live mainly in valley areas covering about 10 per cent of the state. Hill areas cover 89 per cent of the land but have only 20 of the 60 assembly seats, while Meiteis hold 40. Meiteis are restricted from buying land in about 90 per cent of Manipur, whereas tribals can buy land in the Imphal Valley.

subtopics.title: President's Rule: Articles, Duration and Revocation
subtopics.summary: President's Rule is the Centre's takeover of a state government when the constitutional machinery fails, also called State Emergency. A proclamation must be approved by both Houses of Parliament within 2 months, and then continues for 6 months. It can be extended by Parliament up to a maximum of 3 years and can be revoked by the President at any time.

Article 356 lets the President act when a state government cannot function per the Constitution
Article 365 covers a state's failure to comply with directions from the Centre

Resolutions need a simple majority of members present and voting

President can declare that Parliament will exercise state legislature powers

subtopics.title: Key Records and Judicial Review
subtopics.summary: Manipur has had President's Rule the most number of times, 11, followed by UP, J&K and Punjab. The first three instances were in Punjab, PEPSU and Andhra. In S.R. Bommai vs Union of India (1994), the Supreme Court held that the President's power to dismiss a state government is not absolute.

subtopics.title: Vision and Six Pillars
subtopics.summary: Nirmala Sitharaman presented the Union Budget 2026-27 as her record ninth consecutive budget, prepared in the newly inaugurated Kartavya Bhawan. It is framed as a Yuva Shakti-driven blueprint anchored in the Viksit Bharat Vision and guided by three Kartavyas. Six pillars of growth organise the agenda across manufacturing, MSMEs, infrastructure, financial stability and city economic regions.

Pillar 3: Creating champion MSMEs to strengthen the backbone of the economy

Pillar 5: Ensuring long-term security and stability in economic and financial systems

subtopics.title: Manufacturing, Industry and Infrastructure
subtopics.summary: The budget pairs manufacturing schemes for biopharma, semiconductors, containers and critical minerals with infrastructure measures for freight, carbon capture and urban growth. SHAKTI aims to make India a global bio-pharmaceutical manufacturing hub, while the Rare Earth Corridor aims to secure the mining-to-manufacturing value chain. Funds for MSMEs, carbon capture and City Economic Regions complete the package.

CCUS outlay of 20,000 crore to decarbonise hard-to-abate sectors like steel and cement
City Economic Regions: 5,000 crore per region over 5 years

subtopics.title: Agriculture, Services and Women-led Growth
subtopics.summary: Agriculture measures centre on Bharat-VISTAAR, an AI-based platform for accessing farm resources, and on higher-margin plantation crops. Creative and service sectors get talent pipelines and the Orange Economy is promoted, while foreign cloud providers using Indian data centres receive a tax holiday. Women-led development gets community-owned retail outlets and STEM hostels for girls.

subtopics.title: Taxation and Fiscal Framework
subtopics.summary: The budget retained existing income tax slabs for FY 2026-27 and replaces the 1961 Act with a new Income Tax Act 2025 from 1 April 2026. Tax changes include a uniform 2% TCS on LRS remittances and a Minimum Alternate Tax cut to 14%. The fiscal framework sets a deficit target of 4.3% of GDP, record capex of 12.2 lakh crore and a total outlay of 53.47 lakh crore.

Existing income tax slabs retained for FY 2026-27

subtopics.title: Budget Process and Parliament
subtopics.summary: Article 112 requires the annual financial statement to be laid before Parliament, although the word 'Budget' does not appear in the Constitution. The budget is prepared by the Budget Division of the Department of Economic Affairs with NITI Aayog and ministries. Money Bills start in Lok Sabha, and Rajya Sabha can only return them within 14 days without any power to vote on demands for grants.

subtopics.title: Constitution and Role of the Commission
subtopics.summary: The 16th Finance Commission was set up in 2023 under Article 280 to recommend how tax revenue is distributed between the Centre and the States. It has one Chairperson, Dr. Arvind Panagariya, and four other members, appointed by the President for a generally five-year tenure. Its report and an Action Taken Memorandum are laid before Parliament under Article 281, and the Government has accepted its key recommendations for 2026-31.

subtopics.title: Vertical and Horizontal Devolution
subtopics.summary: Vertical devolution fixes the share of the Centre's divisible tax pool transferred to the States, which the 16th Commission kept at 41 per cent. Horizontal devolution decides how that 41 per cent is divided among States, and the revised criteria add GDP contribution while reducing the weight of income distance and geographical area. The divisible pool excludes cesses, surcharges and the cost of collection.

subtopics.title: Grants-in-Aid, Cess and Surcharge
subtopics.summary: Statutory grants under Article 275 go only to States in need of financial assistance and are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India every year. Discretionary grants under Article 282 can be made for any public purpose, and the Centre has no obligation to give them. Cesses and surcharges are levied by the Centre and are not shared with States, while SASCI provides long-term interest-free loans for capital projects.

subtopics.title: Fiscal Discipline and Local Bodies

It also recommends ending off-budget borrowings by States and performance-linked grants for local bodies. For urban areas it proposes an urbanisation premium and a constitutional change regarding State Finance Commission recommendations.

subtopics.summary: The retained 41 per cent share is said to give States revenue predictability, and the revised formula is said to safeguard fiscally weaker States. subtopics.title: Why the CPI base year was revised
subtopics.summary: The Ministry of Statistics & Programme Implementation revised the CPI base year to 2024, replacing the 2012 benchmark. The revision reflects updated consumption patterns, price structures and economic changes since 2012. It uses 2023-24 Household Consumer Expenditure Survey data, and an advisory committee chaired by Biswanath Goldar helped decide the base year.

Ministry of Statistics & Programme Implementation revised the CPI base year.

subtopics.title: What CPI measures and why it matters
subtopics.summary: The Consumer Price Index measures the average change over time in retail prices of goods and services consumed by households. It is the main indicator of retail inflation and is used by the Reserve Bank of India for monetary policy decisions. It also serves as a benchmark for wage revision, pension adjustment and dearness allowance calculation.
facts: CPI measures average change over time in retail prices of goods and services consumed by households.
CPI reflects the cost of living and inflation experienced by consumers.
CPI is the main indicator of retail inflation.
CPI is used by the Reserve Bank of India for monetary policy decisions.
CPI is used for dearness allowance calculation, wage revision and pension adjustment.
Current inflation target is 4%, with a band of 2% (2% to 6%).
Overall inflation in January 2026 (YoY) was 2.75% (provisional).
Rural inflation in January 2026 was 2.73%; urban inflation was 2.77%.
Significance of base revision: better reflection of cost of living, improved monetary policy transmission, greater statistical credibility.

subtopics.title: CPI 2012 versus CPI 2024: key changes
subtopics.summary: The revised CPI 2024 has a larger basket than CPI 2012, with 358 items against 299. It covers online markets, uses the COICOP 2018 classification, and compiles house rent for both urban and rural areas. The food and beverages weightage has been reduced from 45.86% to 36.75%.
facts: Items: 299 (259 goods and 40 services) in CPI 2012; 358 (308 goods and 50 services) in CPI 2024.
Online markets: not covered in CPI 2012; 12 online markets covered in CPI 2024 in cities above 25 lakh population.
Classification: COICOP 1999 in CPI 2012; COICOP 2018 in CPI 2024.
House rent index: only urban areas in CPI 2012; urban and rural in CPI 2024, both excluding employer-provided accommodation.
Data dissemination: combined index only in CPI 2012; rural, urban and combined indices in CPI 2024.
Food and beverages weightage: 45.86% in CPI 2012; 36.75% in CPI 2024.
Formula used: Laspeyres index (base year prices, base year weights, current prices).
Newly added items (January 2026): OTT subscriptions, rural house rent, value-added dairy products, pen drives, babysitting services, fitness equipment, barley products, cleaner fuels.
Removed items: VCR/VCD/DVD players, tape recorders, radios, cassettes, second hand clothing, rope.

subtopics.title: CPI compared with WPI
subtopics.summary: The Wholesale Price Index (WPI) has a base year of 2011-12 and is released by the Office of Economic Adviser, Ministry of Commerce and Industry. The CPI is released by the National Statistical Office (NSO). WPI covers only goods and excludes indirect taxes, whereas CPI covers both goods and services and includes indirect taxes.
facts: WPI base year is 2011-12.
WPI is released by the Office of Economic Adviser, Ministry of Commerce and Industry.
CPI is released by the National Statistical Office (NSO).
WPI includes only goods; CPI includes both goods and services.
WPI excludes indirect taxes; CPI includes indirect taxes.
WPI does not reflect up-to-date expenditure patterns; CPI does.

subtopics.title: Summit Theme, Principles and Objectives
subtopics.summary: India hosted the India AI Impact Summit 2026 at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi, presented as the first multilateral AI summit in the Global South. The summit marked a shift from a Western safety-first model to an impact-first, developmental approach to AI, under the theme 'Sarvajana Hitaya, Sarvajana Sukhaya'. Its work rests on three Sutras and seven Chakras, and it set out four key objectives.
facts: Held at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi; described as the 1st multilateral AI summit in the Global South
Signals a shift from a Western safety-first model to an impact-first, developmental AI paradigm
Theme: 'Sarvajana Hitaya, Sarvajana Sukhaya' (Welfare for All, Happiness for All)
3 Sutras: People (Inclusive Development), Planet (Ethical Innovation), Progress (Sustainable Societal Impact)
7 Chakras (Priority Cooperation Areas): Healthcare, Agriculture, Education, Governance, Climate action, Digital Economy, Social Inclusion
Objective 1: translate global AI discussions into development outcomes aligned with IndiaAI Mission and Digital India
Objective 2: promote responsible and ethical AI, addressing algorithmic bias, privacy protection and accountability
Objective 3: build partnerships between governments, startups, academia and industry
Objective 4: position India as a Global AI Hub and promote an indigenous AI ecosystem
Switzerland will host the 2027 World Summit on AI in Geneva

subtopics.title: New Delhi Declaration and Its Seven Pillars
subtopics.summary: The New Delhi Declaration on AI was adopted at the summit and focuses on inclusive, ethical and development-oriented AI. It is endorsed by 87 countries and 2 international organisations and is built around seven pillars supported by voluntary global initiatives. Separately, the New Delhi Frontier AI Impact Commitments form a voluntary framework signed by frontier AI companies and domestic innovators.
facts: Adopted at the India AI Impact Summit 2026; focuses on inclusive, ethical and development-oriented AI
Endorsed by 87 countries and 2 international organisations (European Union and International Fund for Agricultural Development)
Built around 7 pillars, each supported by voluntary global initiatives
Charter for Democratic Diffusion of AI: promotes locally relevant AI ecosystems and Global South participation
Global AI Impact Commons: platform for sharing successful AI solutions and replicating best practices globally
Trusted AI Commons: repository of tools, benchmarks, safety standards and best practices
International Network of AI for Science Institutions: connects research institutions for collaborative scientific innovation
AI for Social Empowerment Platform: platform for sharing scalable AI solutions for social welfare
AI Workforce Development Playbook & Reskilling Principles: guidance for governments to prepare workforce for AI transformation
Guiding Principles on Resilient & Efficient AI: focus on sustainability and energy-efficient AI systems

subtopics.title: M.A.N.A.V. Roadmap and Previous AI Summits
subtopics.summary: The Prime Minister unveiled the human-centric M.A.N.A.V. Framework for Ethical and Inclusive AI at the summit, with each letter standing for one principle. The booklet also traces earlier global AI summits: the UK's 1st AI Safety Summit and its Bletchley Declaration, the Seoul Summit of 2024 and the 3rd AI Action Summit held in Paris in 2025.
facts: Prime Minister unveiled the human-centric M.A.N.A.V. Framework for Ethical and Inclusive AI at the summit
M: Moral and Ethical Systems; AI must be fair and transparent, subject to human oversight
A: Accountable Governance; clear institutional responsibility, transparent regulatory rules, strong oversight
N: National Sovereignty; securing critical datasets, strengthening domestic compute, indigenous model development
A: Accessible and Inclusive AI; democratise benefits, bridge the digital divide, reach marginalised populations
V: Valid and Legitimate Systems; trust, safety and legal compliance, important given deepfakes and misinformation
UK hosted the 1st AI Safety Summit and adopted the Bletchley Declaration on AI's promises and risks
Bletchley Declaration emphasises aligning AI with human intent, safeguarding rights, safety, ethics and accountability
AI Seoul Summit took place in 2024, co-hosted by the Republic of Korea and the UK government
3rd AI Action Summit was held in 2025 in Paris, France

subtopics.title: Sovereign Models and Domain Platforms
subtopics.summary: India's sovereign AI models include Sarvam's large language models, the Vikram chatbot, Gnani.ai's Vachana speech model and BharatGen's Param2 17B. Bharat GenAI develops foundational models tailored to 22 Indian languages, while BODH, SAHI, VoicERA and BHASHINI cover health and language platforms. The Bio-AI Mulankur Hubs link AI with biotechnology under the BioE3 policy.
facts: Sarvam-30B and Sarvam-105B by Sarvam AI are large language models that generate human-like text
Sarvam's Vikram is a multilingual chatbot for seamless conversations across Indian languages
Vachana is a text-to-speech model by Gnani.ai that supports 12 Indian languages
Param2 17B is a multilingual foundational AI model by BharatGen
Bharat GenAI: India's first government-supported initiative for sovereign foundational AI models, spearheaded by IIT Bombay
Bharat GenAI models are tailored to 22 Indian languages and cover text, text-to-speech and vision-language
BODH: privacy-preserving benchmarking platform for health AI using diverse, real-world health data; positioned under Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission
SAHI (Strategy for Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare for India): national framework for responsible AI integration in healthcare
VoicERA: open-source, end-to-end voice AI stack serving as a national execution layer for multilingual voice AI
BHASHINI (Bhasha Interface for India): AI-powered national language translation and speech platform under Digital India

subtopics.title: Flagship Initiatives, Funding and Global Bodies
subtopics.summary: India's flagship initiatives include the IndiaAI Mission, which builds AI infrastructure around sovereign GPUs, and programmes for startups, women and youth. The summit highlighted large pledges, including $20 billion for frontier deep-tech research. Global context comes from GPAI, established in 2020, and the G7 Hiroshima AI Process, which sets guardrails for advanced AI systems.
facts: IndiaAI Mission: builds AI infrastructure with 10,000 GPUs initially, backed by a budget of 10,372 crore
GPU target: initially 10,000, achieved 38,000, with 20,000 new GPUs being added
IndiaAI Mission 2.0 aims to onboard 38,000 sovereign GPUs and advance the National Compute Portal and strategic compute autonomy
AIRAWAT: India's largest AI supercomputing system at C-DAC Pune, manufactured by Netweb Technologies
AIRAWAT stands for AI Research, Analytics and Knowledge Assimilation
AI for ALL: identifies scalable AI solutions for development challenges, implemented with Startup India
AI by HER: promotes women-led AI innovation, implemented with NITI Aayog's Women Entrepreneurship Platform
YUVAi: encourages AI innovation among youth aged 13-21
$20 billion pledged for frontier deep-tech research
GPAI (Global Partnership on AI): established 2020, officially proposed by France and Canada; secretariat in Paris (OECD); 2024 summit held in India

subtopics.title: Global CPI 2025 Findings
subtopics.summary: Transparency International released the Corruption Perceptions Index 2025, which assesses public sector corruption in 182 countries on a scale from 0 (Highly Corrupt) to 100 (Very Clean). The global average fell to 42, the lowest level in over a decade, signalling worsening corruption trends. Denmark remained the least corrupt country, while only five countries scored above 80.
facts: CPI 2025 assessed public sector corruption across 182 countries.
CPI scale runs from 0 (Highly Corrupt) to 100 (Very Clean).
Transparency International, founded in 1993, released CPI 2025; the index started in 1995.
Global average CPI score declined to 42, the lowest level in over a decade.
About 122 of 182 countries scored below 50.
Denmark ranked 1st with a score of 89.
Denmark has been the least corrupt country for 8 consecutive years.
Only 5 countries scored above 80, compared with 12 a decade ago.
Somalia and South Sudan, each scoring 9, ranked among the most corrupt, along with Venezuela.

subtopics.title: India's CPI 2025 Performance
subtopics.summary: India ranked 91st out of 182 countries with a score of 39 out of 100 in CPI 2025. This is a modest improvement from its 96th rank in 2024, but the score remains below the global average of 42. The source attributes this to persistent governance and accountability challenges.
facts: India ranked 91st out of 182 countries in CPI 2025.
India scored 39 out of 100 in CPI 2025.
India's rank was a modest improvement from 96th in 2024.
India's score remains below the global average of 42.
The booklet links India's position to persistent governance and accountability challenges.
India performs better than Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal and Sri Lanka.
India lags behind countries such as Bhutan and China.

subtopics.title: India's Laws and Agencies
subtopics.summary: India's anti-corruption framework combines statutes such as the Prevention of Corruption Act 1988 and the Right to Information Act 2005 with bodies including the CVC, CBI, ED and CAG. The CVC oversees vigilance administration, while the CBI is the premier investigating police agency for combating corruption in public life. The CAG is the Supreme Audit Institution that helps identify financial mismanagement, corruption or fraud.
facts: Prevention of Corruption Act 1988 provides penalties for corruption by public servants and for abetment of corruption.
Prevention of Money Laundering Act 2002 prohibits use of proceeds of crime in India.
Right to Information Act 2005 gives citizens smoother and greater access to information.
Whistleblower Protection Act 2014 allows registration of corruption or misuse of power against public servants.
Central Vigilance Commission was established in 1964 on K Santhanam Committee recommendations.
CVC was granted statutory status by the CVC Act 2003 and is headquartered in New Delhi.
Central Bureau of Investigation was formed in 1963 and is the premier investigating police agency for corruption in public life.
Directorate of Enforcement was established in 1956 as an Enforcement Unit under the Ministry of Finance.
The CAG is the Supreme Audit Institution under Art 148, appointed by the President.
The CAG holds office for 6 years or up to the age of 65 years.

subtopics.title: International Efforts and Bodies
subtopics.summary: UNCAC 2003 is the only legally binding universal anti-corruption instrument, and India ratified it in 2011. The FATF, set up by the G7 in 1989, acts as a watchdog on money laundering and terrorist financing. INTERPOL, established in 1923, is the world's largest international police organisation, and SDG 16 recognises anti-corruption as an institutional principle.
facts: UN Convention against Corruption 2003 is the only legally binding universal anti-corruption instrument.
India ratified UNCAC in 2011.
G20 Anti-Corruption Working Group (2010) shares effective strategies to combat corruption, especially through emerging technologies.
Financial Action Task Force was established in 1989 by the G7.
FATF has 38 member countries and 2 member organisations: the Gulf Cooperation Council and the European Union.
FATF Black List labels Iran, North Korea and Myanmar as Non-Cooperative Countries or Territories.
FATF Grey List has 21 countries.
SDG 16 acknowledges anti-corruption as an institutional principle.
INTERPOL was established in 1923 and has 196 member countries, including India.
INTERPOL's General Assembly is its highest decision-making body, with one delegate from each member nation.

topics.title: NGT Clears Great Nicobar Mega Infrastructure Project

subtopics.title: Project Overview and Clearance
subtopics.summary: The Great Nicobar Mega Infrastructure Project was launched in 2021, credited to NITI Aayog, and is located on Great Nicobar Island, the southernmost island of India. The National Green Tribunal upheld its Environmental Clearance, citing compliance with Island Coastal Regulation Zone and Coastal Regulation Zone norms. The Andaman and Nicobar Islands Integrated Development Corporation is the implementing agency.
facts: Launched in 2021, credited to NITI Aayog.
Located on Great Nicobar Island, the southernmost and largest Nicobar island.
Indira Point is the southernmost point of India.
Components: International Container Transshipment Terminal, 450 MVA gas and solar-based power plant, dual-use civil-military airport, integrated township.
Strategic importance: near the Malacca Strait, vital to India's Act East Policy and QUAD Indo-Pacific Strategy.
Economic aim: cut reliance on Singapore and Colombo ports.
Implementing agency: Andaman and Nicobar Islands Integrated Development Corporation.
Covered areas include Galathea Bay, Campbell Bay and Great Nicobar, with a Biosphere Reserve and two national parks.

subtopics.title: Environmental and Tribal Concerns
subtopics.summary: The project is criticised for diverting about 130 sq. km of tropical rainforest and cutting nearly 1 million trees. The Environmental Impact Assessment used single-season data, and the proposed afforestation in Haryana cannot replicate the island's rainforest ecosystem. Tribal groups, including the Shompen and Nicobarese, face loss of habitat, cultural disruption and livelihood impact.
facts: About 130 sq. km of tropical rainforest is to be diverted.
Nearly 1 million trees are to be cut.
The Environmental Impact Assessment was based on single-season data.
Concerns exist over inadequate ecological evaluation.
Proposed afforestation in Haryana cannot replicate the tropical rainforest ecosystem.
Shompen (a Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Group) and the Nicobarese tribe are affected.
Concerns include loss of habitat, cultural disruption and livelihood impact.
The island lies in the highest seismic risk zone, vulnerable to earthquakes, tsunamis and climate change impacts.

subtopics.title: Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups
subtopics.summary: A Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Group (PVTG), previously called a Primitive Tribal Group, is a sub-classification of Scheduled Tribes that is more vulnerable than a regular Scheduled Tribe. The Dhebar Commission set up the PTG category in 1973, and the Government renamed these groups PVTGs in 2006. PM-JANMAN, with an outlay of Rs. 24,000 crore, aims to improve their socio-economic conditions.
facts: A PVTG is a sub-classification of Scheduled Tribe that is more vulnerable than a regular Scheduled Tribe.
PVTGs were previously known as Primitive Tribal Groups (PTGs).
The Dhebar Commission established the PTG category in 1973.
The Government of India renamed PTGs as PVTGs in 2006.
Salient features: technological backwardness, stagnant or declining population growth, low literacy, subsistence economy, challenging living conditions.
The Ministry of Tribal Affairs has identified 75 PVTGs across 18 states and one Union Territory.
PM-JANMAN has an outlay of Rs. 24,000 crore.
PM-JANMAN covers safe housing, clean drinking water, sanitation, health and nutrition, and road and telecom connectivity.

subtopics.title: National Green Tribunal
subtopics.summary: The National Green Tribunal is a specialised environmental tribunal set up under the National Green Tribunal Act (2010), and India is the third country after Australia and New Zealand to do so. It provides relief and compensation for environmental damage, applying the polluter pays principle and sustainable development. Its decisions can be appealed in the Supreme Court within 90 days.
facts: Set up under the National Green Tribunal Act (2010).
India is the third country, after Australia and New Zealand, to set up a specialised environmental tribunal.
Principal seat is in New Delhi; regional benches include Bhopal, Pune and Chennai.
Chairperson: a retired Supreme Court judge or High Court Chief Justice, appointed in consultation with the Chief Justice of India.
Judicial members: 10-20, exact number decided by the Central Government.
Hears civil cases under seven laws; excludes the Wildlife Protection Act 1972 and the Forest Rights Act 2006.
Appeals can be filed in the Supreme Court within 90 days.
Appeals must be disposed of within 6 months of filing.
Not bound by the Code of Civil Procedure 1908; guided by natural justice; decisions executable as a civil court decree.

subtopics.title: Why in News: World Wetlands Day 2026
subtopics.summary: World Wetlands Day is observed on 2 February, and the 2026 theme is 'Wetlands and Traditional Knowledge: Celebrating Cultural Heritage'. India's Ramsar Network was expanded when the Union Environment Minister added two new wetlands, bringing the total to 98. Patna Bird Sanctuary in Etah District, Uttar Pradesh, was recognised as the state's smallest bird sanctuary.
facts: World Wetlands Day is observed on 2 February.
The 2026 theme is Wetlands and Traditional Knowledge: Celebrating Cultural Heritage.
Union Environment Minister added two new wetlands to India's Ramsar Network.
India's Ramsar Network total reaches 98.
Patna Bird Sanctuary is in Etah District, Uttar Pradesh.
Patna Bird Sanctuary was established in 1991.
Patna Bird Sanctuary is recognised as the state's smallest bird sanctuary.
Chhari-Dhand Wetland Reserve is in Gujarat's Rann of Kutch.
Chhari-Dhand is famous for Chir Batti night lights across Banni Grasslands.

subtopics.title: Meaning and Classification of Wetlands
subtopics.summary: A wetland is a place where land is covered by water, which may be salt, fresh or in between, and may be seasonal or permanent. The term covers a wide range of water bodies and coastal habitats, from lakes and rivers to mangroves and coral reefs. For classification, wetlands are grouped into three segments.
facts: Wetland: land covered by water that is salt, fresh or in between.
The water cover may be seasonal or permanent.
Includes lakes, rivers and underground aquifers.
Includes swamps, wet grasslands and peatlands.
Includes deltas, tidal flats and mangroves.
Includes coral reefs and other coastal areas.
Wetlands are classified into three segments.
The three segments are Inland, Coastal and Human-made wetlands.

subtopics.title: Ramsar Convention and Montreux Record
subtopics.summary: The Ramsar Convention, formally the Convention on Wetlands of International Importance, was signed in 1971 in Ramsar, Iran, and came into force in 1975. It is the only international treaty addressing a specific ecosystem, and its Conference of Parties meets every 3 years. The Montreux Record, launched in 1990, lists wetland sites where ecological character has changed or is likely to change due to technological developments, pollution or other human interference.
facts: The Ramsar Convention was signed in 1971 in Ramsar, Iran.
The Convention came into force in 1975.
It is the only international treaty addressing a specific ecosystem.
The Convention has 172 member States.
India became a signatory on 1 February 1982.
The Conference of Parties (COP) meets every 3 years.
COP15 took place in 2025 in Victoria Falls, Zimbabwe.
Bolivia has the largest area under Convention protection.
The Montreux Record was launched in 1990 to register sites with changed ecological character.
Keoladeo National Park and Loktak Lake are on the Montreux Record; Chilka Lake was removed.

subtopics.title: Government Initiatives and Wetland City Accreditation
subtopics.summary: Amrit Dharohar is a capacity building scheme between the Ministry of Tourism and the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, aimed at optimal wetland use and nature tourism. The National Wetland Conservation Program is implemented through State Wetland Authorities, and the National Wetland Decadal Change Atlas was prepared by SAC, ISRO. The Wetland City Accreditation Program promotes conservation and wise use of urban and peri-urban wetlands.
facts: Amrit Dharohar is a collaboration of the Ministry of Tourism and the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change.
Amrit Dharohar aims to enhance biodiversity, carbon stock, eco-tourism and local income.
Its primary focus is a shift from High-Volume Tourism to High-Value Nature Tourism at sensitive wetlands.
The National Wetland Conservation Program (1986) is implemented through State Wetland Authorities.
The National Wetland Decadal Change Atlas was prepared by the Space Applications Centre (SAC, ISRO).
The original Atlas was released by SAC in 2011.
A Nature-Culture Tourism Corridor will be developed between Ayodhya and Devi Patan in UP.
Wetland City Accreditation is part of the Ramsar Convention.
Accreditation is granted only to cities meeting all 6 international criteria.
Accreditation is approved at COP 12 (2015) and is valid for 6 years.

subtopics.title: India-France Partnership
subtopics.summary: India and France upgraded their ties to a Special Global Strategic Partnership during the French President's visit. Cooperation spans defence manufacturing, technology, critical minerals, nuclear energy and trade. The 2026 India-France Year of Innovation and the Horizon 2047 roadmap set the course for future ties.
facts: Ties upgraded to Special Global Strategic Partnership during French President's visit
H125 helicopter final assembly line inaugurated at Vemagal, Karnataka (TATA-Airbus)
Joint venture of Bharat Electronics and Safran to produce HAMMER missile in India
2026 is the India-France Year of Innovation; India-France Innovation Network established
Joint declaration to secure diversified, resilient supply chains of critical minerals

France is India's most frequent Republic Day Chief Guest (6th time)
India and France jointly constructing Jaitapur nuclear park in Maharashtra with EDF
Namaste France 2028 to celebrate 30 years of Strategic Partnership

subtopics.title: Chabahar Port and Arab League
subtopics.summary: Iran reaffirmed its commitment to Chabahar Port despite US sanctions uncertainty, and India Ports Global operates the port's terminals. The port gives India a route to Afghanistan and Central Asia that bypasses Pakistan. India and the Arab League also adopted the Delhi Declaration.
facts: Chabahar is Iran's only ocean-facing deep-water port, on the Makran Coast near the Strait of Hormuz
Chabahar is about 550 nautical miles from Gujarat's Kandla Port

India Ports Global assumed operational control of Chabahar Port in 2018

Chabahar is an integral part of the International North-South Transport Corridor
Arab League was established in 1945 in Cairo; it has 22 members including Palestine
Arab States supply over 47% of India's crude oil imports
Over 9 million Indians reside and work in Arab League countries

subtopics.title: Malaysia and Seychelles Visits
subtopics.summary: The Prime Minister's visit to Malaysia produced a joint statement covering defence, digital and trade cooperation. Seychelles' President visited India to announce the SESEL joint vision, marking 50 years of diplomatic relations, along with a USD 175 million assistance package. Both visits stress maritime security and disaster-resilient infrastructure.
facts: India and Malaysia set up a Strategic Affairs Working Group and a Su-30 Forum for air forces
Malaysia-India Digital Council formalised for fintech, AI, cybersecurity and e-governance
RBI and Bank Negara Malaysia to promote local currency settlement
Malaysia is India's 3rd largest trading partner in ASEAN
Harimau Shakti (5th Edition) is a joint military exercise with Malaysia
Malaysia formally acceded to the International Big Cat Alliance
SESEL: Joint Vision for Sustainability, Growth and Security through Enhanced Linkages
India announced a USD 175 million assistance package for Seychelles
Seychelles to become a full member of the Colombo Security Conclave

subtopics.title: Law, Governance and Parliament
subtopics.summary: The Supreme Court questioned WhatsApp's 2021 privacy policy in an appeal against a CCI penalty, flagging data sharing and consent concerns. The topic also covers the Motion of Thanks, the removal procedure for the Lok Sabha Speaker, the Governor's address and the Sahyog Portal. Other items include MTP Act limits, the Frontier Nagaland Territorial Authority and Bharat Taxi.

Supreme Court flagged commercial exploitation of data, abuse of dominant position and lack of informed consent

Delhi High Court: Section 79 safe harbour does not exempt intermediaries from Sahyog Portal compliance
Frontier Nagaland Territorial Authority gets devolved powers over 46 subjects; Article 371(A) unaffected
MTP Act: up to 20 weeks needs 1 registered medical practitioner; 20-24 weeks needs 2
Bharat Taxi is a driver-owned cooperative; 80% of earnings go directly to Sarathis

subtopics.title: Economy, Science, Defence and Space

Two telescope projects in Ladakh will add to India's observatory network.
facts: 10-year government bond yield raised to 6.77%; bond yields and prices move in opposite directions

Digital rupee: e-W for wholesale interbank use, e-R for retail; CBDC food coupon pilot under PDS

India assumed command of Combined Task Force 154, the maritime training task force, for the first time

National Large Solar Telescope: 2-metre aperture, located at Merak (Ladakh)

US launched the FORGE initiative on critical minerals at the Critical Minerals Ministerial

topics.title: Current Affairs February 2026: Defence, Security, Transport, Space and Institutions

subtopics.title: Defence Technology and Missiles
subtopics.summary: The booklet covers a missile test of Agni-III, the Kaveri Engine Programme for military aviation, and the World Defence Show 2026. Agni-III is described with its range, propulsion and payload, while the Kaveri programme is tied to Aatmanirbhar Bharat. The World Defence Show is presented as a biennial global exhibition.
facts: Agni-III was successfully tested from Odisha.
Agni-III is an intermediate-range ballistic missile.
Agni-III is a two-stage solid-fuel missile system.
Agni-III range is beyond 3000 km.
Agni-III payload capability covers conventional and nuclear warheads.

Kaveri Engine Programme progress was reviewed at the Gas Turbine Research Establishment.

subtopics.title: Global Security and Maritime Forums

The UN Office for Disarmament Affairs works on disarmament, and the Indian Army hosted one of its small arms training programmes.
facts: NATO launched the Arctic Sentry mission to enhance security presence in the Arctic region.
Arctic Sentry is led by Joint Force Command Norfolk (JFC Norfolk).

Indian Ocean Naval Symposium was established in 2008 and initiated by the Indian Navy.
IONS is a voluntary and inclusive multilateral forum of navies of the Indian Ocean Region.
India assumed the chairmanship of the Indian Ocean Naval Symposium.
UN Office for Disarmament Affairs was established in 1998 by the UN Secretary-General and is headquartered in New York.

subtopics.title: Transport and Connectivity
subtopics.summary: Kavach is India's indigenous automated train protection system, developed by RDSO and deployed across more than 2200 route km. facts: Kavach is India's Indigenous Automated Train Protection System.
Kavach is deployed across over 2200 route km in India.

subtopics.title: Space and Cyber Security
subtopics.summary: NASA's MESSENGER data revealed bright streaks across Mercury's surface, and the booklet gives key facts about the planet. facts: NASA's MESSENGER data revealed numerous bright streaks scattered across Mercury's surface.
Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun and the smallest planet in the Solar System.
Mercury is the fastest orbiting planet around the Sun.
Mercury is the densest planet after Earth and has no moons or rings.
Key Mercury discoveries: water ice in permanently shadowed polar craters and a large, iron-rich core.
Global CyberPeace Summit 2026 concluded in New Delhi, organised by CyberPeace.
Global Quantum Threat Alliance addresses future cyber risks arising from quantum computing.

quizzes.title: Supreme Court Verdict Practice
quizzes.passage: The Supreme Court of the United States has struck down a set of tariffs that President Donald Trump imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, commonly called IEEPA. The Court's decision was a 6-3 verdict. Chief Justice John Roberts clarified that IEEPA does not allow a President to take unilateral tariff actions without approval from Congress. In his reasoning, the word 'regulate' in IEEPA does not mean 'tax'. The Court observed that IEEPA was designed for emergency economic restrictions, not for general tariff policy. The Court's reasoning focused on the text and purpose of the statute itself. As a result, the Liberation Day tariffs, introduced through an executive order dated 2 April 2025, were invalidated. Before this order, no American President had used IEEPA as a means to impose trade tariffs. The judgment has also raised questions about whether tariffs already collected can be refunded. It has further raised questions about the direction of future American trade policy. Indian exporters are among those affected, since the Liberation Day tariffs had applied to many of their goods. Any broad tariff measure now needs authorisation from Congress, which places a limit on the use of emergency powers for trade protectionism. This is why the verdict is widely discussed in the context of future trade policy.

quizzes.title: Alternative Tariff Laws Recall
quizzes.passage: After the Supreme Court limited the use of emergency economic powers for tariffs, the government had to look to other statutes. The Trade Act of 1974 contains a provision that lets the President impose temporary tariffs. Its purpose is to protect domestic industries and to address trade imbalances or unfair trade practices. The President has used this power to impose a temporary tariff on goods from all countries. A separate provision of the same Act allows action against foreign regulations that unfairly burden American trade. Another route is the Tariff Act of 1930, which permits import tariffs against countries with discriminatory trade practices. The Trade Expansion Act of 1962 allows import restrictions on goods that threaten national security, and this power has been applied to steel and aluminium. Taken together, these laws show that tariff policy can be pursued through specific statutes rather than through emergency powers. Each of these laws addresses a different kind of trade problem, such as a trade imbalance, a threat to national security, unfair foreign regulations or discriminatory trade practices. The government's options therefore depended on matching the legal tool to the specific concern. After the ruling, officials had to choose among these statutes while keeping within the conditions that each one sets out in its own text.

quizzes.title: New START Expiry Check
quizzes.passage: A major nuclear arms control agreement has now reached its end. The New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty, known as New START, expired in early February 2026, leaving no legally binding limits on the strategic nuclear arsenals of the United States and Russia. This ends the last legally binding nuclear arms control pact between the United States and Russia. Earlier arms control efforts had rested on a sequence of agreements, from the ABM Treaty to the later START pacts. Its expiry comes amid worsening geopolitical tensions, and the treaty had originally been signed in 2010 and extended by the Biden administration. The treaty was approaching its final expiry as relations between the two countries deteriorated, particularly because of the Ukraine conflict and growing strategic mistrust. Negotiations have stalled. Russia has suspended the sharing of information about its nuclear forces, citing concerns about possible aggression, while the United States accuses Russia of non-compliance and unreliability. Such a breakdown weakens the transparency and verification that once made nuclear arsenals predictable. Without verified data, both sides may assume worst-case scenarios, and heightened mistrust raises the chance of miscalculation. Historical experience suggests that unchecked arms competition can spiral into conflict. The end of the treaty therefore threatens global strategic stability by amplifying uncertainty and increasing the risk of unintended confrontation.

quizzes.title: India's Nuclear Milestones
quizzes.passage: India's nuclear journey began with an institutional foundation laid under the guidance of a physicist widely regarded as the father of the country's nuclear programme. Within a few years of that foundation, a reactor became operational, marking the first nuclear reactor in Asia. Later, a power plant became the country's first commercial nuclear power station, built with support from the United States and the IAEA. Decades later, India's testing record drew global attention. In May 1998, India carried out a series of nuclear tests at the Pokhran range in Rajasthan's Thar Desert, after an earlier test in the same location. The first tests in that May round were given codenames, and the series was completed in a second round a few days later. India's approach to these weapons has been shaped by its stated policy on their use, which commits it to not striking first. A major turning point came when a group of nuclear suppliers granted India a waiver that allowed nuclear trade, even though India is not a signatory to the Non-Proliferation Treaty. Today India is pursuing a three-stage plan that uses thorium for sustainable power, and a prototype fast breeder reactor is part of that effort. These milestones show how the domestic programme, testing record and diplomacy have developed side by side.

Bangladesh entered a new political phase in February 2026. The Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), led by Tarique Rahman, won the 13th General Election and ended the Awami League's long dominance in the country. The result came after roughly eighteen months of upheaval and marked a major political shift. quizzes.title: July Charter: Typed Answer Practice
quizzes.passage:
Bangladesh's interim government, led by Muhammad Yunus, took part in a major constitutional reform agreement known as the July National Charter. The agreement aims to build what is described as the country's Second Republic and to prevent future authoritarianism. It was signed by a group of political parties together with the interim government, and the reforms were then put to voters in a referendum.

The charter places new limits on the Prime Minister. A lifetime term limit will apply to any individual serving as PM, and the Prime Minister will no longer be able to serve as head of the party and head of government at the same time. The PM also cannot declare a state of emergency alone, because the decision needs written consent from the cabinet and the leader of the opposition.

The charter also changes Parliament. The existing Jatiya Sangsad will become the Lower House, and a new Upper House, called the Senate, will be created. Reserved seats for women in the Lower House will be increased. The Deputy Speaker must be elected from the main opposition party, and a controversial rule that removes MPs who vote against their party will be removed or weakened.

Other changes cover elections and institutions. A non-partisan caretaker government will oversee general elections, and paper ballots will be mandatory. A Supreme Judicial Council and an independent Judicial Appointments Commission are to be formed. Several commissions will receive full financial and administrative independence.

quizzes.title: President's Rule Recall
quizzes.passage: President's Rule is the term used when the Centre takes over the government of a state. The Constitution gives the Centre a duty to make sure that every state government is carried on in accordance with its provisions. When a state's constitutional machinery fails, the Centre can take over under a separate Article, which lets the President issue a proclamation if satisfied that a state government cannot function as the Constitution requires. Such a proclamation is also used when a state does not comply with directions from the Centre. Once a proclamation is issued, Parliament must approve it within a fixed time. If both Houses approve, the arrangement continues for a fixed period. It can be extended, but only with Parliament's approval and only up to an overall limit. During this time, the President can take over the functions of the state government and the powers of the Governor or other executive authorities. The President can also declare that the powers of the state legislature will be exercised by Parliament. A proclamation can be revoked by the President at any time through a later proclamation, and such a revocation does not need Parliamentary approval. Resolutions approving the proclamation in either House need only a simple majority of members present and voting. These rules on duration, approval and revocation are the main points to remember for this topic.

The government has also set a deficit target for the year and expects public debt, measured against the size of the economy, to fall gradually. Capital spending receives special attention because infrastructure investment is seen as a strong multiplier of economic activity. quizzes.title: Devolution and fiscal recall
quizzes.passage: The 16th Finance Commission's recommendations for 2026-31 shape how tax revenue is shared between the Centre and the States. The first stage of sharing is vertical devolution, which fixes the overall share of the Centre's divisible tax pool that States receive. The Commission has kept this share at 41 per cent, the same level set by the previous Commission. The divisible pool covers the Centre's gross tax revenues but leaves out cesses, surcharges and the cost of collection. States have raised concerns that these levies are kept by the Union and not shared, which reduces the untied fiscal space available to them. The second stage is horizontal devolution, which decides how the 41 per cent share is apportioned among individual States. The revised criteria add contribution to GDP as a new parameter, while income distance and geographical area are given less weight. Demographic performance also receives less weight, which has raised fears of an 'Ageing Before Prosperity' problem in some Southern States. The package also seeks fiscal discipline, with the Commission proposing deficit limits for both the Centre and the States by 2030-31. Together, these measures aim to balance fiscal federalism, equity and economic performance.

quizzes.title: CPI revision: reasons and method
quizzes.passage: A price index is useful only when it reflects what people actually buy. An economy changes over time, and so do the habits of households. Consumer spending has become more varied, cities have grown, and many purchases now happen digitally. Services now make up a larger part of household budgets, and families in towns and villages often buy different things. A consumer price index that keeps an old set of items and weights can therefore give a distorted picture of living costs. The statistical agency that compiles the index must periodically revisit the base year, the basket of goods and services, and the weights given to each item. The new base year is chosen with care, using evidence from a recent household expenditure survey and from an advisory committee of experts. Revising the index is a technical task, but its effects are practical. Pay revisions, pension adjustments and policy decisions can all depend on the index. If the index does not match real price changes, these payments and decisions may be wrong. A credible revision therefore helps workers, businesses and governments judge how far household money goes.

quizzes.title: CPI 2024: the numbers behind the changes
quizzes.passage: A consumer price index tracks the prices of a fixed set of goods and services, called the basket, and gives each item a weight. When the index is revised to a new base year, the basket is reviewed so that it matches what households now buy. Several parts of the method change in such a revision. The number of items in the basket can rise, and the split between goods and services can shift to give services a larger place. Prices from online sellers may be recorded directly where the market is large enough to be tracked. The grouping of items into divisions, groups and classes follows an international classification standard, and the newer version is adopted in the revision. Housing is handled separately, through a rent index that depends on what households pay for accommodation. Coverage of this rent index can be widened beyond its earlier scope. The weight given to food is also revised, because household spending has diversified. Finally, the agency decides how widely the results are published. Releasing the index for each state, not only for the country as a whole, gives policy makers a closer view of regional prices. Each of these choices affects how accurately the index measures the cost of living.

Together, these efforts seek to translate high-level global discussions into outcomes that can be measured in development terms. quizzes.title: CPI 2025 Global Picture and Bodies
quizzes.passage: The Corruption Perceptions Index 2025 was released to assess public sector corruption across 182 countries. Each country is placed on a scale from 0 to 100, where 0 stands for highly corrupt and 100 stands for very clean. The global average score fell to 42, which is the lowest level in over a decade and points to worsening corruption trends worldwide. Around 122 of the 182 countries scored below 50, which shows that serious corruption challenges exist in most nations. Denmark placed first with a score of 89, while only five countries scored above 80, compared with twelve a decade ago. This decline suggests an erosion of governance standards even among countries that once performed strongly. India ranked 91st with a score of 39 out of 100, a figure that sits below the global average. Countries such as Somalia and South Sudan, each scoring 9, ranked among the most corrupt, along with Venezuela. The index began in 1995 and is treated as a leading global indicator of public sector corruption. Countries are compared on the same scale, so their positions can be read side by side. quizzes.title: Indian Laws and Agencies Recall
quizzes.passage: India relies on a mix of laws and specialised bodies to fight corruption in public life. The Prevention of Corruption Act penalises corruption by public servants and those who abet it, while the Prevention of Money Laundering Act prohibits the use of proceeds of crime. Citizens gain smoother and greater access to information through a citizen-centric approach to governance. The Central Vigilance Commission oversees vigilance administration and advises the executive on corruption matters. The Central Bureau of Investigation is described as the premier investigating police agency for combating corruption in public life, and it serves as the nodal agency for INTERPOL in India. The Directorate of Enforcement deals with cases related to money laundering by public servants. The Comptroller and Auditor General acts as the Supreme Audit Institution that helps identify financial mismanagement, corruption or fraud. Together these institutions form the backbone of India's governance and accountability framework, although the booklet notes that persistent challenges remain. Each body works within its own mandate, and together they support the country's broader efforts against corruption. The Right to Information Act is one of the tools that gives citizens a more open route to government information. Public servants, who are the focus of several of these laws, face penalties when they engage in corruption.

quizzes.title: Project and Clearance Practice
quizzes.passage: The Great Nicobar Mega Infrastructure Project has returned to the spotlight after the National Green Tribunal upheld its Environmental Clearance. The Tribunal found that the project complied with the coastal norms that apply to the island. Great Nicobar is the largest island of the Nicobar group and sits at the southern end of India, where a dense green cover of trees meets long coastlines. Planners see the project as a major step in building trade and strategic capacity near the Malacca Strait. Officials argue that the plan will bring jobs, better connectivity and new economic activity to the islands. Critics, however, have questioned whether the damage to the island's fragile ecology can be offset. The island is also home to tribal communities whose way of life depends on the land and the sea. This debate highlights a familiar challenge in India: how to balance national economic and strategic goals with the protection of ecologically sensitive regions and their people. Understanding the project therefore requires knowing about the island's location, its ecology, the people who live there and the legal bodies that review such proposals. Local residents and planners will need to show how the development protects both the forest cover and the people who depend on it.

quizzes.title: Concerns and Tribal Facts
quizzes.passage: The Great Nicobar project has raised serious environmental and social concerns. Clearing large stretches of dense forest would remove habitat for wildlife and disturb an ecosystem that has developed over long periods. Critics argue that the environmental study relied on too little field data, so it may not capture how the island's species behave across changing conditions. Compensatory afforestation has been proposed in a different state, but critics say a new plantation cannot reproduce the unique structure and species of a natural forest. Indigenous communities are at the centre of the debate. Certain tribal groups are considered especially vulnerable, and they depend on the forest for food, shelter and cultural practices. Any disturbance could cause loss of habitat, disruption of traditions and a hit to local livelihoods. The island is also exposed to natural hazards. Earthquakes, tsunamis and the impacts of climate change add to concerns about building large facilities there. Supporters point to strategic and economic gains, but the debate shows how difficult it is to weigh development against ecological and tribal rights. Whether the project proceeds responsibly will depend on how well the safeguards are enforced in practice. Supporters and critics alike agree that the island's natural and human heritage needs careful protection. Clear rules on monitoring and accountability would help build trust among the communities that are most affected.

quizzes.title: Wetlands and the Ramsar Framework
quizzes.passage: Wetlands are places where land is covered by water, whether the water is salt, fresh or somewhere in between, and whether the cover is seasonal or permanent. The category is broad, and every form of water cover described here is treated as part of one wetland definition. It includes lakes, rivers, underground aquifers, swamps, wet grasslands and peatlands, along with deltas, tidal flats, mangroves, coral reefs and other coastal areas. For classification, wetlands are divided into three segments. The international framework that protects these ecosystems is a treaty that deals with one specific type of habitat. Its formal name is the Convention on Wetlands of International Importance, and it is the only international treaty that addresses a specific ecosystem. Its members meet at a Conference of Parties. Wetland sites that fall under it are known as Ramsar Sites, and India is one of the signatories. A separate register tracks wetland sites where ecological character has changed, is changing, or is likely to change. Such changes can result from technological developments, pollution or other human interference. A site entered on this register shows that its ecological character is under pressure. World Wetlands Day is observed each year, and each year carries its own theme that draws attention to wetland care.

quizzes.title: Schemes, Atlas and Accreditation
quizzes.passage: India's wetland policy combines conservation with tourism and local livelihoods. Under one capacity building scheme, a tourism ministry works with the environment ministry to make better use of wetlands. The scheme aims to enhance biodiversity, carbon stock, eco-tourism opportunities and income for local communities. Its primary focus is a shift from crowded visits to higher-value nature tourism at ecologically sensitive wetlands. Conservation at the national level is carried out through state-level bodies. A national atlas of decadal wetland change documents how these wetlands have changed over time, and an original version of that atlas was released by a national space agency unit. Such records help authorities see which wetlands have altered over a decade. The programme is run jointly, so the planning of wetland use and the study of wetland change are both part of one national effort. Tourism is also being planned along cultural routes. A new corridor will connect Ayodhya with another place in the same state, combining cultural visits with nature, and the corridor is announced as a new route in the state. Cities are recognised too. quizzes.title: Parliament, Governor and Speaker
quizzes.passage: Each year, Parliament opens its work with a formal address. At the start of the first session each year, the President addresses both Houses of Parliament assembled together. The address informs Parliament of the reasons for its summons and sets out the policies and legislative agenda of the elected government. After the address, a motion of thanks is moved in the Lok Sabha and discussed. Members may move amendments that express regret or disapproval, for example by pointing to important issues that the address has omitted. Passing the motion indicates the House's confidence in the government. State legislatures follow a similar pattern, with the Governor delivering an address to the Legislative Assembly. The Governor acts as a constitutional head, so the address reflects the policies of the elected government and not the personal opinion of the Governor. The Speaker of the Lok Sabha holds a different kind of office. The House can remove the Speaker through a resolution, but the process requires advance notice and a formal listing in the business of the House. While the removal is under consideration, the Speaker faces specific limits on the role they can play in the House. These rules show how the Constitution balances the roles of the elected government, the presiding officers and the constitutional heads.

quizzes.title: Research, Space and Maritime Security
quizzes.passage: India is investing in science, space and maritime cooperation at several levels. A new fund under the Anusandhan National Research Foundation is designed to carry research from the laboratory to industrial-scale manufacturing. Its focus areas include biotechnology, artificial intelligence, deep tech and advanced manufacturing, and it is meant to reduce import dependence. In space, the Union Budget has approved two major telescope projects in Ladakh, a region chosen for its high altitude, clear skies and minimal light pollution. One project will study the Sun, including solar magnetism and space weather, while the other will look at exoplanets, the early universe and galaxy evolution. Maritime security is also addressed through the Combined Maritime Forces, a voluntary multinational partnership headquartered in the Gulf region that aims to protect sea lanes and prevent piracy and smuggling. India has taken on a larger role in this partnership by commanding one of its task forces for the first time, with a focus on training and capacity building. Together, these developments show how India links research, infrastructure and security. Each initiative relies on cooperation between government agencies, industry and international partners to deliver long-term results for the country. Such schemes are meant to strengthen domestic capability, support new industries and reduce dependence on imports in strategic sectors.
